newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel leader to visit refugee crisis city.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel leader to visit refugee crisis city.

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila, whose forces are accused by international aid agencies of trying to exterminate 100,000 Rwandan refugees, said on Saturday he was going to north-east Zaire to tackle the crisis.
The U.N. says the rebels, who control the eastern half of Zaire, have chased the unwanted Rwandan Hutus into the jungle to starve.

Secretary-General Kofi Annan has called it a policy of "slow extermination," and a U.N. food agency spokeswoman, making a comparison with Hitler's Germany, said: "The expression 'Final Solution' is not exaggerated."

Kabila, head of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, told Reuters in an interview he would go to the north-eastern city of Kisangani over the weekend to direct a hands-on probe.
He said he would consult Western diplomats, the United Nations and aid agencies as well as his aides in Kisangani on a lasting solution for nearly 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees.
The refugees are the rump of the two million people who fled Rwanda three years ago fearing reprisals for a mass slaughter of Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
Most of the 1994 refugees have returned to Rwanda and those that remained vanished this week from camps in which the rebels had cut them off from international aid and contact with news media.
"I will go to Kisangani in order to get to the root of this problem and to also come up in consultation with western diplomats, the United Nations and aid agencies, with a lasting solution," he said.
The guerrilla chief once again reiterated his call for an independent investigation into the biggest crisis to beset his movement since he first launched Africa's latest war six months ago.
"I am for a clean and independent investigation into this whole saga. I seek and demand the truth only," he added.

Kabila, whose forces control about half of Africa's third largest and potentially richest nation, said he stood by his earlier invitation to the United Nations to set up an independent probe team into the refugee crises.
The rebel chief said a big group of the refugees were former soldiers and militia "still armed to their teeth and using the refugee cause to hide their criminal activities".
Kabila said he stood by his promise to discipline his troops should a probe team find them guilty of excesses.
"My troops are very disciplined. But I am more than willing to take stern measures against any of them found guilty of excesses," he said.
He added: "So far the facts before me suggest my troops only intervened to stop fighting between heavily armed refugees and local Zaireans."
Kabila spoke as aid workers said they would use all means at their disposal to find the refugees, many of whom are accused of taking part in the genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994.

"We will use all means at our disposal to find them. We need more information from the (rebel) alliance," said U.N. refugee agency UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg in Kisangani, capital of the north-east.

"On Saturday, we will either use new flights or travel down overland. One problem is that the forest is so dense that even on Friday when we saw plumes of smoke from the air we circled over it and could not tell who it was coming from," he added.
A U.N. aerial search confirmed on Friday that some 85,000 Rwandan refugees fled into the jungle earlier this week from camps at Kasese and Biaro, 45 km (25 miles) south of Kisangani.
UNHCR said earlier it had received reports suggesting Biaro had been emptied. A U.N. mission to Kasese, 25 km (15 miles) south of Kisangani on Thursday found no refugees, alive or dead.
Kasese camp, which last week had 55,000 refugees, had been sealed off for four days from aid workers and journalists.
The UNHCR spokeswoman said agencies were also blocked from Biaro but an aid worker trapped there on Tuesday reported a train-full of rebels arriving followed by looting and fighting.
The aid worker said the Hutus left Biaro soon afterwards.
In Geneva, aid agencies expressed outrage at rebel treatment of the refugees, who fled Rwanda in 1994 and are collectively accused by minority Tutsis of genocide in Rwanda the same year.

But some analysts accused the United Nations of waging massive propaganda against Kabila's rebels, saying many of the refugees still in Zaire were part of a hard-core armed group willing to fight to the end.
"Many of them have nothing to lose. They form part of a hard-core criminal group ready to fight, to kill to the end in the name of refugee sanctuary," said a mining expert in Lubumbashi.
Another one added: "Human memory is so short that just three years after Rwanda's genocide the killers are now being pictured as the saints, the hunted, victims. It is sickening."

Phil Doherty, an MSF project manager for the Great Lakes region, told Reuters an MSF team to the area between March 26 and April 3 had not seen rebels killing refugees but rebels were on the watch for Hutu former Rwandan troops and militiamen.

The rebels say they only intervened at Kasese refugee camp outside Kisangani after it was attacked by Zairean villagers in revenge for the killing of six local people. They say a rebel force was then ambushed by former Rwandan troops and militiamen.
